prompt:
Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Document units:
S097: The Helitack Crew Leader uses the Crewline Mobile Tablet to acknowledge air-to-ground instructions and report whether crews are inside any planned drop or reconnaissance area.
S098: The Caldera Incident Command Portal displays crew acknowledgements beside aviation tasks so the Air Attack Supervisor can verify that ground resources are clear before authorizing flight activity.
S099: If the Confirmed Ignition State is active and airspace approval is delayed, the system keeps suppression planning visible while preventing premature aircraft dispatch.
S100: Coordination records are retained with timestamps, participant identities, and radio path status so post-incident review can reconstruct both aviation decisions and interagency notifications.
S101: This section defines how the system converts detection observations, aerial imagery, weather updates, and geospatial overlays into a shared fire behavior assessment for operational use.
S102: The assessment begins when visual detections are correlated with incident geometry, terrain, fuel type, and current resource locations in the mapping workspace.
S103: North Lookout Camera Mast captures a time-stamped smoke column bearing and reports the pan, tilt, zoom, and confidence values needed to project the observation onto terrain.
S104: South Lookout Camera Mast supplies a separate bearing track so the mapping workflow can triangulate a probable origin area and bound the uncertainty ellipse.
S105: The Smoke Classifier Module assigns each observation a smoke likelihood, growth trend, and obscuration flag before the result is made available for analyst review.
S106: The Duty Detection Officer uses the spot snippet to compare the automated classification with visible flame, smoke color, and terrain context before accepting the observation into the assessment queue.
S107: Drone imagery is treated as a higher-resolution confirmation layer when weather, airspace, and communications conditions permit flight operations.
S108: The Drone Tasking Service packages approved imaging objectives as map footprints, altitude bands, and revisit intervals so the requested coverage can be compared with the active perimeter model.
S109: The Drone Pilot Operator uses the swap ticket to keep imaging sorties aligned with available aircraft endurance and expected return time.
S110: Frames collected during a sortie are orthorectified against the terrain model and registered to the incident grid before they are used for perimeter adjustment.
S111: The Sentinel Fireline Analytics Engine identifies heat signatures, smoke edges, flame fronts, and potential spot fire indicators in the registered imagery.
S112: Analytic results are not displayed as final fireline until confidence thresholds, sensor age, and positional error are applied as explicit map attributes.
S113: The MesoWest Weather Fusion Node ingests station observations, forecast grids, and local quality checks to maintain the wind, humidity, temperature, and stability fields used by the spread model.
S114: Brindle publishes a time-indexed weather update that marks significant forecast changes and identifies which map products require recomputation.
S115: Weather fields are interpolated across the incident area with terrain-aware weighting so ridge, drainage, and slope effects are represented at operational map scale.
S116: Geospatial overlays include fuels, slope, aspect, roads, structures, water sources, jurisdiction boundaries, evacuation zones, and known communications coverage.
S117: The fire behavior model combines the accepted perimeter, recent growth vectors, weather fields, and fuel conditions to estimate short-term spread direction and rate.
S118: Model output is expressed as probability bands rather than a single line so supervisors can see both the most likely path and the practical planning margin.
S119: Emberhall renders the current perimeter, projected spread, resource positions, and decision annotations into a common operating picture with role-based symbology.
S120: The Caldera Incident Command Portal produces the Crew Staging Pin from the approved map layer and assigns it an effective time, location accuracy, and incident identifier.
S121: Operational recommendations are generated from rule checks that compare projected fire arrival times with values at risk, road access, crew travel time, and aircraft availability.
S122: Recommendations may include confirming an ignition, increasing camera monitoring, requesting drone coverage, preparing aviation options, repositioning ground crews, or notifying county partners.
S123: The Air Attack Supervisor receives map products that emphasize projected columns, flight hazards, target areas, and timing constraints without obscuring ground resource information.
S124: The County Emergency Liaison receives a simplified view that preserves perimeter confidence, threatened areas, and recommended public safety coordination actions while hiding tactical details not needed for civil coordination.
S125: Every map product records source time, processing time, model version, analyst acceptance, and supersession status so users can distinguish current guidance from archived assessments.
S126: When inputs conflict, the common operating picture shows the conflict explicitly and requires review before the affected recommendation is promoted for command use.
S127: Suppression planning begins after the Caldera Incident Command Portal promotes an accepted fire location into the operational map and marks it available for aviation review.
S128: The Air Attack Supervisor reviews the promoted location, the confidence history, and the current airspace status before authorizing reconnaissance or retardant planning.
